Lessons.Title: Area of Rectangles — Count Square Units Using Rows and Columns
ExplanationParagraphs: First-edition IM K–5 (2021), Grade 3 Unit 2 Lesson 4, source Goal: describe and find rectangular area (within 60 square units) by counting congruent unit squares in rows and columns. The original Student Task Statements PDF has four pages and thirteen source instructional figures, all source mathematical geometry individually inspected. First-party Edulytics content is independently written; original source pictures, including the proprietary partner illustration, are not embedded.

Warm-up, Which One Doesn't Belong: Area and Arrays (10 minutes): original A a 4-row by 5-column tiled rectangle of twenty square regions, B four rows by six columns (24 square cells) with a black dot inside each square, C four rows by five columns of 20 isolated dots (object array), D five groups of four dots (20 objects). B differs by total (24 rather than 20), but further explanations may distinguish area units from dots, grid arrangement and separate circled groups. Teacher asks multiple defensible explanations, and records vocabulary row, column, group, grid and rectangle.

Activity 1 What Did I Create? (20 minutes): each PAIR of students receives a folder or solid obstruction and two paper grids of 12 by 12 squares. Partner A secretly draws a rectangle with equal square cells, describes its number of rows and columns WITHOUT disclosing the total number of unit squares, while B constructs what the description implies, without seeing A's paper. Compare both drawings, discuss what was similar and different, SWITCH roles and repeat. The mathematical core is precise row-and-column language, not the computed area; human teacher evidence is mandatory. Original Representation: Access for Perception models this no-looking procedure physically before the pair activity.

Activity 2 Find the Area (15 minutes): four different original diagrams require area in square units and an explanation. ORIGINAL FIGURE 1 = two rows of nine (18 square units), FIGURE 2 = six rows of five (30), FIGURE 3 = six rows of TEN (60), FIGURE 4 = five rows of nine (45). Third figure has been visually inspected: the 6×10 grid resolves the prior unverified-source gap. Do not substitute an invented 3rd area. Encourage counting by ones, twos, fives or tens, as appropriate, and verify with another grouping.

MLR8 Discussion Supports during Activity 2 asks partners to restate another student's strategy using 'area', 'square units', 'row' and 'column'; partner explanations count as teacher-judged work. The original teacher note for 30 units also suggests three groups of ten as an alternative arrangement, which does not change the result. Numeric responses 18/30/60/45 can be checked, but explanation, accurate grouping and requested square-unit label require human review.

Lesson synthesis compares three rows of two separate dots (array counting OBJECTS) with a three-by-two square-tiled rectangle (measuring covered SPACE). Ask students to describe area, methods of area measurement, and lingering questions in their own words. The original section summary includes a tiled rectangle of four rows of six, area 24 square units, and warns that gaps or overlaps invalidate a tiling.

Original 2021 teacher preparation suggests optional centers Can You Build It? Stage 1 (Rectangles) and Five in a Row Multiplication Stage 1 (factors 1–5 and 10). Teacher reflection concerns whether class norms promote engagement from every learner. The original educator-gated Cool-down 'What's the Area?' is NOT copied. Edulytics's separate first-party rectangle Cool-down remains a skill equivalent with teacher-observed drawing, not a publisher task duplicate. No Stage D, CI, tests, merge or deployment carried out.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area of a tiled rectangle
KeyConcepts.Definition: The total two-dimensional plane space covered by congruent square tiles.
KeyConcepts.Rule: After checking no gaps or overlaps, rows × square units per row counts the total area in square units.
KeyConcepts.Example: 6 rows of 10 unit squares cover 60 square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rows, columns and commutative counting
KeyConcepts.Definition: Both horizontal and vertical equal groupings describe the same rectangle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use clear row/column language without confusing it with total area before completing partner challenge.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 6×5 grid can be counted by six groups of five or three groups of ten, both total 30.

KeyConcepts.Title: Separate objects from regions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A dot array counts objects; a tiled rectangle measures covered area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Identical numeric products do not make the referents identical.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3×2 dots count 6 objects, whereas a 3×2 tile region has area 6 square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Hidden partner rectangle instructions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A learner can communicate an area model precisely without showing it.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not reveal the total square count or drawing to partner B; tell rows and columns, then compare both sketches and swap.
KeyConcepts.Example: 'Draw 4 rows with 7 squares per row' is acceptable; 'area is 28' is not the launch instruction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original warm-up four pictures
WorkedExamples.Question: Which original picture differs by count, which pictures differ by how objects or area are represented?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count groups using the source geometric arrangements.
Steps: Source A: four rows by five square cells = 20 area units.
B: four rows by six square cells with central dots = 24.
C: four rows of five isolated dots = 20 objects.
D: five separately outlined groups of four dots = 20 objects.
Justify at least two possible 'doesn't belong' answers.
WorkedExamples.Answer: B alone contains 24; A/C/D contain 20, but other justifications possible.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teachers review mathematical precision and source picture identity.

WorkedExamples.Title: Partner reconstruction, no answer disclosure
WorkedExamples.Question: How can partner B draw the same 4-by-7 rectangle without seeing it?
WorkedExamples.Method: Give structure but NOT total tile count.
Steps: A draws a four-row seven-column tiled rectangle on a hidden 12×12 grid.
A says: there are four horizontal rows of seven congruent squares.
B draws with paper screen still between partners.
After comparison they reflect on the instructions, then switch roles.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Valid matching geometric drawings; do not initially tell B the number 28.
WorkedExamples.Check: This is human-observed; numeric grading cannot certify procedure.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four exact original rectangular areas
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute the four original original 2021 source images in square units.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count by congruent unit-square rows and columns.
Steps: Explain a second counting method and include 'square units'.
WorkedExamples.Check: Source images individually reviewed, original art not reused; teacher reviews labels and methods.

WorkedExamples.Title: Array of dots versus area
WorkedExamples.Question: What is different about an array of 3×2 objects and a 3×2 tiled rectangular region?
WorkedExamples.Method: Name the quantity the model measures.
Steps: Separate dot array contains six individual objects.
The filled rectangle has six congruent unit squares covering its plane region.
The numerical answer alone does not convey what is being measured.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 6 objects versus 6 square units of area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Guessing source rectangle 3 has no known area.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 2021 original SVG shows six rows and ten columns of congruent unit squares.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Saying 24 dots are 24 square units of area.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source B puts dots inside square cells, while C/D are object arrangements; the referent differs.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Name whether counting objects or measuring covered region.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Revealing total area to partner B at Activity 1 launch.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source deliberately blocks the drawings and total to practice precise row/column descriptions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Describe group structure only until sketches are complete.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Writing a bare integer as complete explanation of a source area diagram.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity requires units and showing why the grid has the area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record '60 square units' and show six groups of ten.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Measuring rectangle by boundary length rather than its tiled area.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Length and area have different mathematical units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count the congruent squares covering the full plane region without gaps.

SummaryPoints: First-edition 2021 original four-page student PDF and thirteen actual source image files visually inspected on authorized Our-CS.
Warm-up A=20 square cells, B=24 dot-marked square cells, C=20 separate dots, D=20 dots in five groups of four; multiple correct WODB rationales.
Source Activity 1 is a hidden-pair 12×12 grid reconstruction using rows/columns without revealing total, then switch roles.
Four original figures: 2×9=18; 6×5=30; third 6×10=60; 5×9=45 square units.
Source 2021 MLR8, Representation accessibility and source section summary must be respected.
Original student construction and peer reasoning always require teacher review, whereas first-party supplemental numeric checks do not auto-pass whole task.
No publisher original artwork or restricted cooldown copied; tests/CI/Stage D unexecuted.
